name: East Kewa
confidence_why: Yarapea 2006, a doctoral grammar of East Kewa by a native speaker, gives predictable initial stress on words of up to three syllables, second-syllable stress on four-syllable words and third-syllable stress on longer ones, and explicitly rejects the earlier first-hand statements of Franklin and Franklin 1962 and Franklin 1978 that verb stems are stressed by tone class and that stems of over four syllables take second-syllable stress; with only that older description in dissent and no third source, the reading is well founded but rests on one modern grammar.

new_statements.quote: Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) Stress is non-phonemic and occurs usually on the first syllable of words. There are two contrastive tonemes: high tone and low tone. With some words the tone of the first syllable adapts top the last tone of the preceding word. In other word-classes also other adaptions take place, and with some words the tone always stays the same. The tone is not written. [...] Conventions: Orthographic [...] The tone is phonemic, but is not written.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kewa (sheet covers West and East Kewa; SIL record files it under East Kewa kjs) has two contrastive level tonemes (high, low; phonemic but not written in the orthography); word stress is non-phonemic and usually falls on the first syllable of the word.
new_statements.exceptions: only the hedge 'usually' on first-syllable stress; no word classes or word lengths singled out (the longer-word placements 2nd syllable in 4-syllable words / 3rd syllable in 5+-syllable words that the catalog codes from Yarapea 2006 sec. 2.2.1 are not mentioned); tone sandhi noted: in some words the first-syllable tone adapts to the last tone of the preceding word, other adaptations by word class, some words tonally invariant.
new_statements.identity_note: The sheet is titled 'Kewa Language' (Mendi, Southern Highlands Province) and treats Kewa as one language with dialect-labelled example blocks: consonant examples '(West Kewa)', vowel examples '(East Kewa)', one '(East Kewa only)' item, and orthographic conventions for sounds that 'occur only in East Kewa' (<ny>, <ty>); the SIL Archives record 42473 files it under subject language East Kewa [kjs]. The suprasegmental statement is given for Kewa as a whole, not per dialect. Yarapea 2006 (the catalog's basis) describes Kewapi, his East Kewa variety.

tone_statements.quote: This paper provides a preliminary analysis of the tone system in East Kewa. The domain of tone in East Kewa is the morpheme, but like other New Guinea Highlands languages tone sandhi applies such that the tone of each morpheme affects the tone of the following morpheme. [...] Phonemic lexical tones are usually written as H (high) and L (low). M is used for phonetic mid tone in certain cases where H and L are neutralised. [...] The Franklins suggest that West Kewa has four tone melodies, H, L, HL, and LH. [...] This analysis works well for East Kewa if it is restricted to root forms, but not when it is applied to verb + desinence combinations [...]
tone_statements.locator: Abstract p. 294; sec. 1 p. 295 (H/L/M notation); sec. 3.1 'Tone and the phonological word' p. 296

tone_statements.summary: 2 tones H/L (surface M by neutralisation); word-level tone melodies (nouns 5 classes incl. toneless and floating-H; verb roots 3 classes + desinence melodies, LHL possible); domain = morpheme, rightward tone sandhi across morphemes/words; no role for stress in the analysis.

readall_conflicts: The one listed work could not be read, so no new source-vs-catalog disagreement arises from it. Among the East Kewa sources already held by the project there is a real, documented disagreement that the catalog entry silently resolves in Yarapea's favour: Yarapea 2006 (Morphosyntax of Kewapi, ANU thesis, sec. 2.2.1, pp. 28-30) gives initial stress for 1-3 syllable words, second-syllable stress for 4-syllable words, third-syllable stress for words of more than four syllables, secondary stress on the penult of words over five syllables, and states that these rules hold for all word classes ("Verbs, for example, do not show stress patterns that are different to nouns"). Franklin & Franklin 1962 (Kewa I, sec. 2.1.2.3, reprinted in PL C-53 p. 29; file say instead: "Stress is non-phonemic. The most pronounced stress occurs on the first syllable of words, except verbs where it may occur elsewhere.. Affixation of tone Class I verbs causes stress to shift to final stem syllable. Tone Class I verb stems are stressed on the second syllable", and Franklin & Franklin 1978 (PL C-53, p. 18 as cited by Yarapea) say "a primary stress occurs on the first syllable of any noun stem of less than four syllables and on the second syllable of any stem over four", which differs from Yarapea's third-syllable rule for 5+ syllable words. Yarapea 2006 explicitly notes and rejects the Franklins' verb exception. The catalog rule string encodes Yarapea's version only.

tone.quote: There are three tone classes for Kewa verbs. In order to show that grammatical subclassification of verb stems does not coincide with the phonological tone subclassification, one verb from each stem class has been chosen and the affix tones have been written morphophonemically on Charts A-D. ... Affixes on Chart E have tone patterns as they would occur with Tone Class I stems (basic low tone). For a more detailed description of the tone system see Franklin (1962).
